topics.title: Alzheimer's Disease & Dementia
topics.summary: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, a group of conditions in which memory, thinking and daily functioning gradually decline. Other causes of dementia include vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia and frontotemporal dementia.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Alzheimer's disease involves the build-up of abnormal proteins (amyloid and tau) that damage and kill brain cells. Age is the strongest risk factor, along with family history, genes, head injury, and heart and blood vessel disease.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Alzheimer's disease and other dementias typically begin with trouble remembering recent events, then progress to confusion, difficulty with language and planning, mood and personality changes, and eventually need for help with everyday care.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, is diagnosed by a doctor using history from the person and family, memory and thinking tests, blood tests to exclude other causes, and brain scans. Some specialist tests can look for Alzheimer's-related proteins.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: There is no cure for Alzheimer's disease, but some medicines can ease symptoms for a time. Support, structured routines, treatment of other health problems and care for family carers are central to managing dementia.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Alzheimer's disease is progressive, but its pace varies between people. Staying physically and mentally active, not smoking, limiting alcohol, and controlling blood pressure, diabetes and hearing loss may lower the risk of dementia.

What is the difference between dementia and Alzheimer's disease?
Can Alzheimer's disease be prevented or slowed down?

topics.title: Parkinson's Disease
topics.summary: Parkinson's disease is a long-term progressive disorder of the nervous system that mainly affects movement. It develops when nerve cells in a part of the brain that produces dopamine gradually die.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Parkinson's disease results from loss of dopamine-producing brain cells, and the exact cause is usually unknown. Risk rises with age, and genes and some environmental exposures may play a part. It is somewhat more common in men.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Parkinson's disease causes tremor at rest, slow movement (bradykinesia), muscle stiffness and balance problems. Non-movement symptoms such as constipation, poor sleep, low mood, reduced sense of smell and memory changes are also common.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Parkinson's disease is diagnosed mainly by a specialist doctor from symptoms and a neurological examination, as no single blood test confirms it. Scans or other tests may be used to rule out other conditions.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Parkinson's disease cannot be cured, but medicines that replace or mimic dopamine can control symptoms well for many years. Physiotherapy, speech therapy and exercise help, and surgery such as deep brain stimulation is an option for some people.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: There is no proven way to prevent Parkinson's disease. It progresses slowly over many years, and with good treatment and support many people live for a long time with a good quality of life. Regular exercise is widely encouraged.

topics.title: Epilepsy
topics.summary: Epilepsy is a long-term neurological condition in which abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain cause repeated seizures. Seizures can range from brief lapses of awareness to convulsions with loss of consciousness.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Epilepsy can result from brain injury, stroke, infection, brain tumours, developmental conditions or inherited factors, but in many people no cause is found. Epilepsy can begin at any age, most often in childhood or older adulthood.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: The main symptom of epilepsy is recurrent seizures, which may involve shaking, stiffening, staring, odd sensations, confusion or collapse. Symptoms depend on which part of the brain is affected and whether the seizure spreads.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Epilepsy is diagnosed from a detailed description of the seizures, often from a witness, together with an electroencephalogram (EEG) recording brain activity and a brain scan such as MRI. Blood tests may help exclude other causes.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Epilepsy is usually treated with anti-seizure medicines, which control seizures in most people. Surgery, nerve stimulation or special diets may help when medicines are not enough. Call emergency services if a seizure lasts more than five minutes.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Many people with epilepsy become seizure-free with treatment and live full lives. Taking medicines regularly, sleeping well, avoiding known triggers and following local rules on driving and safety reduce risks. Preventing head injury can lower the chance of some epilepsy.

sample_questions: What causes epilepsy?
What should I do if someone has an epileptic seizure?
Can epilepsy be cured or controlled with medication?

topics.title: Migraine
topics.summary: Migraine is a common neurological condition that causes recurring, often severe headaches, typically with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people also experience warning symptoms called aura before the headache.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Migraine is linked to changes in brain activity and nerve signalling, and it often runs in families. Common triggers include stress, poor or irregular sleep, skipped meals, hormonal changes, certain foods or drinks, and strong sensory stimuli.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: A migraine usually causes a throbbing headache, often on one side, with nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. Aura can involve flashing lights, blind spots or tingling, and attacks may last from hours to days.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Migraine is diagnosed mainly from the pattern of symptoms and a doctor's examination. Scans are not usually needed unless the headaches are unusual, sudden and severe, or accompanied by other neurological signs. A headache diary can help.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Migraine attacks are treated with pain relief and specific migraine medicines taken early, plus rest in a quiet dark room. For frequent attacks, preventive medicines and avoiding triggers may help. Seek urgent care for a sudden, worst-ever headache or weakness.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Migraine cannot be cured, but attacks can often be reduced by regular sleep, meals and exercise, stress management and trigger avoidance. For many people migraine becomes less frequent with age, and it is not usually dangerous.

What is the difference between a migraine and a normal headache?
How is migraine treated and prevented?

topics.title: Multiple Sclerosis
topics.summary: Multiple sclerosis is a long-term condition in which the immune system attacks the protective covering (myelin) of nerves in the brain and spinal cord, disrupting messages between the brain and body.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: The exact cause of multiple sclerosis is unknown, but it is an immune-mediated condition. Risk is higher in young adults, women, people with a family history, those with low vitamin D, past Epstein-Barr virus infection, and smokers.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Multiple sclerosis can cause fatigue, vision problems, numbness or tingling, weakness, balance and walking difficulty, bladder problems and thinking changes. Symptoms often come in relapses followed by recovery, though some people have steady progression.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Multiple sclerosis is diagnosed by a specialist using symptoms, a neurological exam and MRI scans showing areas of nerve damage. Tests of spinal fluid and nerve signals may help, and other conditions must be ruled out.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Multiple sclerosis cannot be cured, but disease-modifying treatments can reduce relapses and slow progression. Steroids help treat relapses, and physiotherapy, rehabilitation and medicines for specific symptoms improve daily life.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: There is no known way to prevent multiple sclerosis. Outlook varies widely, and modern treatment has improved it. Not smoking, staying active and keeping a healthy lifestyle support wellbeing in people living with multiple sclerosis.

topics.title: Depression
topics.summary: Depression is a common and treatable mental health condition marked by persistent low mood or loss of interest in activities, lasting weeks or longer and affecting daily life, work and relationships.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Depression has no single cause. It can arise from a mix of genetic, biological, psychological and life factors, such as stressful or traumatic events, loss, long-term illness, loneliness or a family history of depression.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Depression can cause persistent sadness, loss of interest or pleasure, tiredness, changes in sleep or appetite, poor concentration, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, and sometimes thoughts of self-harm. Anyone with such thoughts should contact emergency services or a crisis line right away.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Depression is diagnosed by a doctor or mental health professional through a conversation about symptoms, their length and impact, often with a questionnaire. Blood tests may check for physical conditions that can mimic depression.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Depression is treatable with talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, antidepressant medicines, or both, along with support, exercise and good sleep. Most people improve with treatment, and seeking help early is encouraged.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Depression can recur, but many people recover fully and learn ways to stay well. Staying connected with others, being active, sleeping well and getting early help for low mood can lower the risk of depression returning.

topics.title: Anxiety Disorders
topics.summary: Anxiety disorders are a group of mental health conditions involving excessive, persistent fear or worry that is out of proportion to the situation and interferes with daily life. They include generalised anxiety, panic disorder, phobias and social anxiety.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Anxiety disorders arise from a combination of genetics, brain chemistry, personality and life experiences. Stressful or traumatic events, a family history of anxiety, long-term illness, and caffeine or substance use can raise the risk.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Anxiety disorders can cause constant worry, restlessness, irritability, trouble sleeping and concentrating, and physical signs such as a racing heart, sweating, trembling and breathlessness. Panic attacks bring sudden intense fear with these symptoms.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Anxiety disorders are diagnosed by a doctor or mental health professional after discussing symptoms, how long they last and how they affect life. Physical causes such as thyroid problems may be checked to exclude other explanations.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Anxiety disorders respond well to talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, and sometimes to medicines such as certain antidepressants. Relaxation techniques, regular exercise and reducing caffeine and alcohol can also help.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Anxiety disorders are common and treatable, and many people improve substantially with help. Learning coping skills, managing stress, staying active and seeking support early may reduce how severe anxiety becomes or how often it returns.

How are anxiety disorders treated?

topics.title: Bipolar Disorder
topics.summary: Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition causing marked shifts in mood, energy and activity, with episodes of elevated mood (mania or hypomania) and episodes of low mood. It is treatable and manageable long term.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Bipolar disorder is strongly influenced by genetics and brain function, and it often runs in families. Stressful life events, sleep disruption and substance use can trigger episodes. It commonly first appears in late teens or early adulthood.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Bipolar disorder involves highs, with raised mood, little need for sleep, racing thoughts and risky behaviour, and lows with sadness and low energy. Anyone with thoughts of self-harm should contact emergency services or a crisis line right away.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Bipolar disorder is diagnosed by a mental health specialist from the history of mood episodes, often with input from family. It can be mistaken for depression alone, so a past history of high mood is carefully asked about.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Bipolar disorder is usually treated with mood-stabilising medicines, sometimes with other medicines, together with talking therapy and education about the condition. Regular routines, good sleep and early recognition of warning signs help prevent episodes.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Bipolar disorder is a lifelong condition, but with ongoing treatment and support many people live stable, fulfilling lives. Taking treatment consistently, keeping regular sleep and avoiding alcohol and drugs reduce the chance of relapse.

topics.title: Schizophrenia
topics.summary: Schizophrenia is a long-term mental health condition that affects how a person thinks, feels and perceives reality. It can involve hallucinations, delusions and disorganised thinking, and it is treatable with ongoing support.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Schizophrenia is thought to result from a mix of genetic vulnerability and environmental factors, including differences in brain development. Family history, complications around birth, heavy cannabis use and severe stress may increase risk. It is not caused by poor parenting.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Schizophrenia can cause hallucinations such as hearing voices, false fixed beliefs (delusions), confused speech and thinking, and reduced motivation, emotion and social withdrawal. Symptoms usually begin in late adolescence or early adulthood.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Schizophrenia is diagnosed by a psychiatrist based on symptoms, their duration and impact on functioning. Tests and sometimes scans help rule out other causes such as substance use or physical illness.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Schizophrenia is treated with antipsychotic medicines together with talking therapy, family support, and help with housing, work and social life. Early treatment improves outcomes, and many people achieve good recovery with continuing care.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Schizophrenia cannot yet be reliably prevented, but early help after first symptoms improves the outlook. With steady treatment and support, many people manage symptoms and live independently. Avoiding recreational drugs lowers the risk of relapse.

topics.title: ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder)
topics.summary: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition marked by ongoing patterns of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that are greater than expected for age and interfere with daily life. It affects children and adults.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: ADHD is strongly influenced by genetics and differences in brain development, and it often runs in families. Premature birth, low birth weight and some exposures in pregnancy may add risk. It is not caused by bad parenting or too much sugar.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: ADHD can cause difficulty paying attention, being easily distracted, forgetfulness, restlessness, constant movement, talking a lot and acting without thinking. Symptoms start in childhood and may continue into adulthood, often looking different with age.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: ADHD is diagnosed by a specialist after a detailed assessment of symptoms in more than one setting, such as home and school or work, and their effect on life. There is no single test for ADHD.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: ADHD is managed with a combination of approaches, including behavioural strategies, parent and teacher support, education, and for many people medicines that help attention and impulse control. Organisation skills and routines are also useful.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: ADHD cannot be prevented, but early recognition and support improve school, work and relationships. Many people with ADHD thrive with the right strategies and treatment, and some symptoms lessen with age.

topics.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder
topics.summary: Autism spectrum disorder is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference affecting how a person communicates, interacts socially and experiences the world, often with focused interests and repetitive behaviours. It varies widely between individuals.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Autism spectrum disorder arises mainly from genetic factors affecting early brain development, often running in families. Some pregnancy and birth factors may contribute. Vaccines do not cause autism spectrum disorder, a point firmly established by research.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Autism spectrum disorder can involve differences in social communication, such as eye contact and understanding unspoken cues, plus repetitive actions, strong routines, intense interests and unusual sensitivity to sounds, lights or textures. Signs often appear in early childhood.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Autism spectrum disorder is diagnosed by specialists, such as paediatricians, psychologists or psychiatrists, through observation, developmental history and structured assessments. There is no blood test, and diagnosis can occur in childhood or later in adult life.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Autism spectrum disorder is not an illness to be cured, but support can help, including communication and social skills therapy, educational adjustments, behavioural support and treatment of related conditions such as anxiety or sleep problems.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Autism spectrum disorder cannot be prevented. With early understanding, tailored support and accepting environments, autistic people can develop strengths and lead fulfilling lives, though the level of support needed differs greatly between individuals.

topics.title: Insomnia
topics.summary: Insomnia is a common sleep disorder in which a person has trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, despite having the chance to sleep, leading to daytime tiredness and difficulty functioning.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Insomnia can be triggered by stress, anxiety, depression, irregular schedules, caffeine, alcohol, noise, certain medicines, pain or other health conditions. Risk rises with age, and short-term insomnia can become long-lasting through habits and worry about sleep.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Insomnia causes difficulty getting to sleep, waking during the night, waking too early, and unrefreshing sleep. It often leads to daytime tiredness, low mood, irritability, poor concentration and a higher risk of accidents.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Insomnia is diagnosed mainly from a description of sleep problems and their effect on daytime life, often with a sleep diary. Doctors check for medicines, health conditions or other sleep disorders, such as sleep apnoea, that may be responsible.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Insomnia is best treated first with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and good sleep habits, such as regular times and a calm bedroom. Medicines may sometimes help for short periods but are generally not the first choice.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Insomnia often improves with treatment, and prevention focuses on regular sleep times, daytime activity, limiting caffeine, alcohol and screens before bed, and managing stress. Persistent insomnia lasting weeks is worth discussing with a doctor.

topics.title: COVID-19
topics.summary: COVID-19 is an infectious respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, first identified in late 2019. It ranges from no symptoms to severe pneumonia and can occasionally cause long-lasting effects.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus and spreads mainly through tiny respiratory droplets and aerosols from infected people. Older age, weakened immunity, obesity and long-term conditions such as heart or lung disease raise the risk of severe COVID-19.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: COVID-19 symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, tiredness, aches, headache and loss of taste or smell. Some people have no symptoms, while others develop shortness of breath; seek urgent care for breathing difficulty or chest pain.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: COVID-19 is diagnosed with a test of a nose or throat sample, either a rapid antigen test or a more sensitive laboratory PCR test. Testing helps confirm infection and guide isolation and treatment.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Most people with COVID-19 recover at home with rest, fluids and medicines for fever and pain. Antiviral treatments may be offered to people at higher risk, and severe COVID-19 may need hospital care and oxygen.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: COVID-19 is prevented by staying up to date with vaccination, good ventilation, hand hygiene, and staying home when unwell. Most people recover fully, though some develop long COVID with symptoms lasting weeks or months.

topics.title: Influenza (Flu)
topics.summary: Influenza is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. It occurs in seasonal outbreaks, usually causes sudden fever, aches and cough, and can be serious in older adults, young children and people with other illnesses.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Influenza is caused by influenza viruses, mainly types A and B, which spread through coughs, sneezes and contaminated surfaces. Influenza is more serious in older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with chronic conditions or weak immunity.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Influenza typically begins suddenly with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, tiredness, dry cough and sore throat. It is usually more severe than a cold. Seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or persistent high fever.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Influenza is often diagnosed from symptoms during flu season. A swab of the nose or throat can confirm influenza with a rapid or laboratory test, which is mostly used in hospital or for people at higher risk.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Influenza in healthy people usually improves with rest, fluids and medicines to ease fever and aches. Antiviral medicines can be given, especially to high-risk people or those seriously ill, and work best when started early.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Influenza is best prevented by yearly vaccination, which is updated to match circulating viruses. Hand washing, covering coughs and staying home when sick also help. Most people recover within one to two weeks, though complications such as pneumonia can occur.

How long does influenza last?

topics.title: Common Cold
topics.summary: The common cold is a mild, very frequent viral infection of the nose and throat. It causes a runny or blocked nose, sneezing and sore throat, and usually clears up on its own within about a week to ten days.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: The common cold is caused by many different viruses, most often rhinoviruses. It spreads through droplets from coughs and sneezes and by touching contaminated surfaces. Young children, crowded settings and weakened immunity make the common cold more likely.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: The common cold causes a runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, sore throat, mild cough and sometimes a low fever or mild headache. Symptoms usually peak in two to three days and fade within about ten days.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: The common cold is diagnosed from its typical symptoms, and tests are not normally needed. A doctor may check if symptoms suggest another illness, such as influenza, a bacterial infection or allergy.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: There is no cure for the common cold, and antibiotics do not work because it is caused by viruses. Rest, fluids and simple remedies for pain, fever and congestion ease symptoms while the body recovers.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: The common cold is best prevented by regular hand washing, avoiding touching the face and keeping away from people who are sick. Recovery is almost always complete; see a doctor if symptoms last more than a couple of weeks or breathing becomes difficult.

topics.title: HIV/AIDS
topics.summary: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system's CD4 cells, weakening the body's defences. Without treatment it can progress to AIDS, the late stage of infection, but modern treatment allows people to live long, healthy lives.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: HIV spreads through unprotected sex, sharing needles, transmission from mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding, and rarely through infected blood. HIV does not spread through hugging, shared food, or everyday contact.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: HIV may cause a flu-like illness with fever, rash and swollen glands soon after infection, then often few symptoms for years. Untreated HIV weakens immunity, leading to AIDS with severe infections, weight loss and certain cancers.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: HIV is diagnosed with blood or saliva tests that detect antibodies, antigens or the virus itself. Testing is quick, widely available and confidential, and regular testing is advised for people at higher risk of HIV.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: HIV is treated with antiretroviral therapy, a combination of medicines taken daily that reduces the virus to very low levels. HIV cannot yet be cured, but effective treatment protects health and stops sexual transmission to others.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: HIV can be prevented with condoms, never sharing needles, testing, and preventive medicines such as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). With early diagnosis and ongoing treatment, people with HIV can expect near-normal life expectancy.

topics.title: Malaria
topics.summary: Malaria is a life-threatening disease caused by Plasmodium parasites, spread to people by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It is mainly found in tropical and subtropical regions but is preventable and curable.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted by infected Anopheles mosquitoes. Travelling to or living in areas where malaria occurs is the main risk, and young children, pregnant women and people with low immunity are most vulnerable to severe malaria.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Malaria typically causes fever, chills, sweating, headache, muscle aches and vomiting, usually starting one to several weeks after a bite. Severe malaria can cause confusion, seizures, anaemia and organ failure and needs emergency care.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Malaria is diagnosed with a blood test, either examining a blood smear under a microscope or using a rapid diagnostic test. Anyone with fever after travel to a malaria area should be tested promptly.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Malaria is treated with antimalarial medicines, chosen according to the parasite species, severity and local drug resistance. Prompt treatment usually leads to full cure, while severe malaria requires hospital care and medicines given by injection.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Malaria is prevented by avoiding mosquito bites with bed nets, repellent and covering clothing, and by preventive medicines for travellers. Vaccines now exist for children in affected regions. Early treatment gives an excellent outlook.

topics.title: Dengue
topics.summary: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection common in tropical and subtropical regions. It causes high fever and body pain and usually resolves on its own, but a minority of cases become severe and need urgent care.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Dengue is caused by dengue viruses, of which there are four types, spread by the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. Living in or travelling to warm, humid areas with dengue raises risk, and a second infection with a different type increases the chance of severe dengue.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Dengue typically causes sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea and rash. Seek urgent care if severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding or extreme drowsiness develops as the fever falls.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Dengue is diagnosed with blood tests that detect the virus or the body's antibody response, combined with symptoms and recent travel or exposure. Blood counts help monitor for falling platelets and other warning signs.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Care focuses on rest, plenty of fluids and fever and pain relief, with medical monitoring. Severe dengue needs hospital care with fluid support, and some pain medicines that raise bleeding risk are avoided.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Dengue is prevented mainly by avoiding mosquito bites and removing standing water where mosquitoes breed. Vaccines exist in some countries for selected groups. Most people recover in about one to two weeks, and early care greatly improves outcomes in severe dengue.

topics.title: Measles
topics.summary: Measles is a highly contagious viral illness causing fever, cough and a characteristic rash. It can lead to serious complications, especially in young children, but it is largely preventable with vaccination.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Measles is caused by the measles virus, which spreads very easily through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People who are unvaccinated, young children, pregnant women and those with weakened immunity are most at risk of measles.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Measles begins with fever, runny nose, red eyes and cough, followed a few days later by a red blotchy rash that spreads from the face downward. Small white spots inside the mouth may appear. Complications include ear infection, pneumonia and brain inflammation.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Measles is suspected from the typical symptoms and rash, and confirmed with a laboratory test of blood, throat swab or urine. Cases are reported to public health authorities so contacts can be protected.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: There is no specific antiviral treatment for measles. Care includes rest, fluids and fever relief, and treating complications such as pneumonia. Vitamin A is recommended by the World Health Organization for children with measles in some settings.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Measles is prevented by two doses of the measles-containing vaccine, usually the MMR vaccine, which is safe and highly effective. Most people recover in a couple of weeks, but measles can be fatal, particularly in undernourished young children.

topics.title: Chickenpox & Shingles
topics.summary: Chickenpox and shingles are both caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Chickenpox is an itchy blistering rash illness, usually in childhood, while shingles is a painful rash that appears when the dormant virus reactivates later in life.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Chickenpox and shingles are caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Chickenpox spreads easily through the air and by contact with blisters. After recovery the virus stays dormant in nerves, and shingles can occur with older age or weakened immunity.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Chickenpox causes fever and an itchy rash of fluid-filled blisters that crust over. Shingles causes burning pain followed by a band of blisters on one side of the body, sometimes leaving lasting nerve pain.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Chickenpox and shingles are usually diagnosed by a doctor from the typical appearance and pattern of the rash. Laboratory tests on a swab from a blister can confirm the diagnosis if it is uncertain.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Chickenpox is usually managed with rest, fluids, soothing lotions and fever relief. Shingles may be treated with antiviral medicines started early and with pain relief. People at higher risk may need antivirals for chickenpox too.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Chickenpox is prevented by the varicella vaccine, and a separate shingles vaccine is offered to older adults in many countries. Most people recover fully from chickenpox and shingles, though shingles can cause long-lasting nerve pain.

topics.title: Typhoid Fever
topics.summary: Typhoid fever is a bacterial infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread through contaminated food and water. It causes prolonged fever and abdominal symptoms and is treatable with antibiotics.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi, spread by food or water contaminated with the faeces of an infected person. It is most common where sanitation and clean water are limited, and travellers to such areas are at risk.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Typhoid fever causes a high fever that rises gradually, with headache, weakness, stomach pain, and constipation or diarrhoea. Some people develop a rash. Untreated typhoid fever can lead to serious complications such as intestinal bleeding or perforation.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Typhoid fever is diagnosed by finding the bacteria in a blood culture, or sometimes in stool or bone marrow samples. Doctors consider recent travel to affected areas when assessing prolonged fever.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Typhoid fever is treated with antibiotics, along with fluids and rest. Resistance of the bacteria to some antibiotics is a growing problem, so the choice depends on local patterns and test results. Severe typhoid fever may need hospital care.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Typhoid fever is prevented by vaccination, safe drinking water, good sanitation, careful food hygiene and hand washing. With prompt antibiotic treatment most people recover fully, though some can carry the bacteria without symptoms.

topics.title: Sepsis
topics.summary: Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency in which the body's response to an infection injures its own tissues and organs. Fast recognition and treatment greatly improve the chances of survival.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Sepsis is triggered by an infection, most often of the lungs, urinary tract, skin or abdomen, caused by bacteria and sometimes viruses or fungi. Babies, older adults, pregnant women, and people with weak immunity or long-term conditions are at higher risk of sepsis.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Sepsis can cause fever or low temperature, fast heart rate and breathing, confusion, extreme weakness, very low urine output, clammy or mottled skin and low blood pressure. Sepsis is an emergency, so call emergency services immediately if suspected.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Sepsis is diagnosed by clinical assessment of vital signs and organ function, supported by blood tests including cultures, lactate and kidney and liver tests. Doctors also look for the source of infection with other tests and scans.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Sepsis needs urgent hospital treatment with antibiotics given as early as possible, intravenous fluids and oxygen. Severe sepsis may need intensive care, medicines to support blood pressure and organ support, and the source of infection may need removal.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Sepsis is reduced by preventing infection through vaccination, good hygiene, wound care and prompt treatment of infections. Many people recover from sepsis, but others have lasting effects such as fatigue, and severe sepsis can be fatal.

topics.title: Antibiotic Resistance
topics.summary: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria change so that antibiotics no longer kill them or stop their growth. It makes infections harder to treat and is a major global public health threat.

sections.label: Causes & risk factors
sections.text: Antibiotic resistance develops when bacteria are exposed to antibiotics, and it is accelerated by overuse and misuse, such as taking antibiotics for viral illnesses, not finishing prescribed courses, and heavy use in farming. Poor hygiene helps resistant bacteria spread.

sections.label: Symptoms
sections.text: Antibiotic resistance does not cause its own symptoms. Instead, resistant infections show up as illnesses that fail to improve or worsen despite usual antibiotic treatment, with longer illness, more complications and a higher chance of hospital stays.

sections.label: Diagnosis
sections.text: Antibiotic resistance is detected in the laboratory by growing bacteria from samples such as blood, urine or wounds and testing which antibiotics work against them (susceptibility testing). Results help doctors choose effective treatment.

sections.label: Treatment
sections.text: Antibiotic-resistant infections are treated with other antibiotics that still work, often stronger, more toxic or given by injection, guided by laboratory results. Some resistant infections have very few options left, which is why new treatments are needed.

sections.label: Prevention & outlook
sections.text: Antibiotic resistance is slowed by using antibiotics only when prescribed and as directed, never sharing them, vaccination, hand washing and infection control in hospitals. Antibiotic resistance is a growing global threat, so coordinated action is needed.
